title: Can a linear probe trained on one jailbreak category generalize to unseen categories?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: poor cross-category generalization means deployers must continually collect labeled data for new harm types, undermining the 'low cost' advantage. Strong generalization supports that probes detect a general 'harmfulness' feature. Directly deployment-critical finding.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Leave-one-category-out cross-validation with logistic regression is a standard ML evaluation technique. StrongReject provides pre-categorized prompts. All computation is lightweight. A motivated beginner with basic Python/ML knowledge can execute this.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: 6 folds of leave-one-out cross-validation, AUROC per fold, comparison to full-data and keyword baselines. Single precise experiment with well-defined deliverable (generalization table). Minimal dependencies, obvious success criteria.

novelty.reasoning: Cross-category generalization of jailbreak probes has been partially studied. 'What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs?' (BlackboxNLP 2025) found linear and non-linear probes have limited ability to classify held-out attack methods. JBShield demonstrated strong transferability across unseen jailbreaks with only 30 calibration samples. However, the specific leave-one-category-out cross-validation design using StrongReject's 6 harm categories with AUROC per fold and comparison to baselines is a focused systematic evaluation not directly replicated. The general finding (poor linear probe generalization) is known; the proposed systematic StrongReject-based evaluation adds incremental value.
